summary: Costa Rica lies in Central America. It abolished its army in 1948 and is known for its stable democracy, environmental conservation and rich biodiversity.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Christopher Columbus reached this coast on his fourth voyage in 1502, and in the 1560s the Spanish founded towns such as Cartago in the Central Valley; Catholicism arrived with colonization and became the only legally permitted faith. The “Virgin of the Angels” (La Negrita), discovered in Cartago in 1635, became the country’s patron, and every year on 2 August hundreds of thousands make the pilgrimage on foot. The 1949 constitution still retains Catholicism as the state religion, but with the rise of evangelicalism and secularization the share of believers has declined steadily since the late 20th century.

ranking.name: Protestant / Evangelical
ranking.description: Jamaican laborers brought in to build the Atlantic Railway and the banana plantations in the late 19th century introduced the Baptist, Methodist and Anglican churches to Limón Province on the Caribbean coast. From the 1970s and 1980s, Pentecostal and charismatic churches influenced by American missionaries expanded rapidly on the urban periphery and in the countryside, emphasizing personal faith and mutual-aid networks and attracting many former Catholics to convert, forming the roughly one-quarter share of the population seen today.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Costa Rica ranks among the highest in Central America in literacy and urbanization, and younger generations, shaped by higher education and internet culture, identify less with church authority. Since the 21st century, social debates over the separation of church and state and over same-sex marriage (legalized in 2020) have also led many people to no longer identify with any denomination; the non-religious are concentrated in the San José metropolitan area.

ranking.name: Other religions
ranking.description: These include Jehovah’s Witnesses and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons), mostly introduced by American missionary activity in the 20th century. There are also a Jewish community that immigrated around the 1930s, Buddhism and folk beliefs brought by Chinese immigrants, and the traditional beliefs preserved by indigenous peoples such as the Bribri; all are very small in number.

religion.background: Spanish colonization in the 16th century brought Catholicism into the Central Valley; both during the colonial period and after independence (1821), the Catholic Church was part of the state system, and the 1949 constitution still defines it as the state religion, making Costa Rica one of the few countries in the Americas that still has an established church. Jamaican immigrants on the Caribbean coast brought Protestantism in the late 19th century, but it was long confined to Limón. In the late 20th century evangelical churches expanded rapidly, while the spread of education and urbanization markedly increased the non-religious population, turning the religious landscape from “almost entirely Catholic” into one of diverse coexistence.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish colonists settled in the Central Valley from the mid-16th century, and the indigenous population there fell sharply because of disease and warfare, so Spanish became the common language of the whole country. Costa Ricans make heavy everyday use of the formal “usted,” while “vos” survives in colloquial speech, and they are fond of diminutives ending in -tico, so “Tico” became the nickname for the nationals. Today schools, the media and the government all operate in Spanish.

ranking.name: Limón Creole English
ranking.description: Beginning in 1871 the construction of the Atlantic Railway to the Caribbean coast, and later the banana plantations of the United Fruit Company, brought in large numbers of Jamaican laborers, whose English-based Creole took root in Limón Province. Residents of African descent were long confined to the Caribbean coast, and only the 1949 constitution confirmed the citizenship of those born there; since then they have integrated into mainstream society, and the younger generation has largely switched to Spanish, so the number of speakers has gradually declined.

language.history: Before colonization the region had indigenous languages of the Chibchan family, such as Bribri, Cabécar and Maleku, which are still spoken by a few people and protected by law. After Spanish colonization in the 16th century, Spanish spread with the agricultural settlements of the Central Valley and became the sole national language after independence in 1821. The Jamaican immigrants brought by the railway and banana industry in the late 19th century formed an English-based Creole in Limón. Since the 20th century the spread of national education has made Spanish the mother tongue of almost everyone, and the growth of tourism has also made English an important second language.

ranking.name: Gallo pinto
ranking.description: Leftover white rice from the previous day is stir-fried with black beans, onion, sweet pepper and cilantro, then drizzled with the national sauce, Salsa Lizano; it is often eaten for breakfast with fried eggs, sour cream and fried plantain.
ranking.history: The combination of rice and beans reflects the union of rice introduced in the colonial period with beans native to the Americas, and the “rice and beans” of the Afro-Caribbean coast also had an influence. The name means “spotted rooster,” describing the speckled look of black beans mixed with white rice; Costa Rica and neighboring Nicaragua both claim to be its birthplace, and the two countries have even held contests to make the largest serving of gallo pinto. Salsa Lizano, which appeared in 1920, later became its indispensable seasoning, giving the dish a distinctly Costa Rican flavor. Today it is found at breakfast from home kitchens to hotels and is regarded as a symbol of national identity.

ranking.name: Casado
ranking.description: A set plate that includes white rice, black beans, a green salad and fried plantain, together with grilled chicken, pork chop, beef or fish; the portions are generous and the price modest.
ranking.history: The casado is the most common lunch at the small family restaurants known as “sodas” in Costa Rica, and its combination originated in the high-calorie home-style meals needed by workers on coffee and banana plantations. The name means “married man”; a common explanation is that a man going to a restaurant hopes to eat food like what his wife makes at home, while others say it is because rice and beans are always paired together as if “married.” It condenses the country’s agricultural food tradition built on rice, beans and plantain, and remains an everyday meal for office workers and laborers.

ranking.name: Chifrijo
ranking.description: White rice, stewed black beans and fried pork chunks (chicharrón) are layered in a cup, topped with tomato-and-onion salsa (pico de gallo), and eaten by scooping it up with tortilla chips.
ranking.history: The name is a blend of “chicharrón” (fried pork) and “frijoles” (beans). It is generally believed to have been created in the late 20th century by Miguel Cordero, the owner of a bar in Tibás, a suburb of San José, as a snack to accompany beer; he later even registered the name as a trademark. By recombining traditional rice and beans with fried pork into a bar snack, it quickly became popular in bars and restaurants across the country and is one of the representatives of contemporary Costa Rican everyday food.

ranking.name: Olla de carne
ranking.description: Bone-in beef is simmered for a long time with a variety of root vegetables such as cassava, corn, plantain, chayote and taro, producing a clear, sweet broth.
ranking.history: This stew combines the Spanish colonists’ tradition of the beef stew (cocido) with the cassava, corn and tuber crops that Native Americans had long cultivated. In the colonial period the Central Valley was dominated by a smallholder economy, so a single pot of stew that could feed a whole family became a weekend dish on farms. The name literally means “meat pot”; it remains a signature dish of family Sunday lunches and also often appears on the table in the cold, rainy season.

ranking.name: Arroz con pollo
ranking.description: Shredded chicken is cooked together with rice, carrots, sweet peppers and peas, colored golden with annatto (achiote), and often served with potato chips and Russian salad.
ranking.history: Arroz con pollo originated in Spain; like Valencian paella, it can be traced to the rice cultivation promoted by the Moors on the Iberian Peninsula in the Middle Ages, and it was carried to Latin America in the colonial period. Costa Rica replaced expensive saffron with annatto, long used by indigenous peoples, to color it, producing a local version. Because one big pot can serve many guests, it became a must-have dish at birthdays, weddings and church events, and serving it with potato chips is a custom peculiar to Costa Rica.
